content.p: On the night of 12 February 1992, armed men entered Bara, a village in Gaya district in the Indian state of Bihar, and over the next hours tied up and killed dozens of men belonging to the Bhumihar caste. The Supreme Court of India later counted 35 dead. According to the court, the attackers shouted slogans for the Maoist Communist Centre (MCC) as they left, and the court held them to be members of that group, now called CPI (Maoist). The killings belong to a long cycle of caste violence in central Bihar, and PUDR, a civil-liberties group, calls Bara the only massacre case in which the anti-terror law was applied and upheld.

The case did not end with the killings or with the first verdict. Four men were sentenced to death in 2001, and by 31 January 2017, according to PUDR, the President had commuted their sentences to life imprisonment. Critics, among them a group of academics and activists, have argued that the trial under an anti-terror law was unfair and that the caste of the condemned shaped the outcome. What follows is what the court found, what reporters suspected at the time, and what the critics said.
content.h2: A district already at war with itself
content.p: Central Bihar in the early 1990s was a place where landowning castes, landless labourers and armed groups on several sides were killing one another. India Today, reporting a fortnight after the massacre, described it as a sign that caste wars had taken on a new dimension. The magazine tied the political atmosphere to Laloo Prasad Yadav, who had launched a campaign for social justice the year before and, in the magazine's words, had mobilised the militant backward castes to strengthen his political base.

India Today reported that the MCC's strike was ostensibly a reprisal for the killing of 10 Harijans in the neighbouring villages of Maine and Barsimha on 23 December 1991. A private army of Bhumihar landlords, the Swarna Liberation Front, was suspected of involvement in that killing. The magazine quoted the Front's chief, Ramadhar Singh "Diamond", as saying it had killed over 100 extremists. But the magazine also noted that the administration was surprised, because Bara itself had not been involved in the December killings.

The Indian Express, looking back in 2016, wrote that the massacre was believed to be the fallout of six earlier killings in 1990 and 1991 in which 59 Scheduled Caste men and agricultural labourers died. It added that in 1997 upper-caste attackers carried out what it called a revenge attack for Bara, leaving 58 Dalits dead at Laxmanpur-Bathe.

The fullest account of the night comes from the Supreme Court's judgment, which summarises the first statement given to police by a villager, Satendra Kumar Sharma. According to that statement, recorded in the early hours of 13 February, he was about to go to bed at about 9.30 p.m. when he heard firing and bomb blasts and saw the village on fire. A group of 10 to 15 unknown men came to his door, saying they wanted two named men. Out of fear he opened it, and he was taken to a temple on the north-eastern edge of the village, where his father, two uncles and four brothers were already sitting with their hands tied behind their backs. Between 50 and 60 armed people guarded them. Groups of 15 to 20 men went house to house bringing more villagers. One of the attackers said no male should be left alive.

Women arrived weeping at the temple, and one attacker told them to go home. Then, the statement says, the men were taken to a canal, their hands and legs tied, and killed by cutting their necks with a pasuli, a sharp cutting weapon. Hearing that the police were coming, the attackers began to flee, and Sharma escaped with his life. When police went to the canal with him they found 35 named people dead and others seriously wounded, who were sent to hospital.

The statement alleged that the attackers carried police rifles, that some wore police uniforms, and that there were about five hundred of them, two to three hundred armed. As they left they shouted slogans for the Maoist Communist Centre. The judges later accepted that the attack had been planned: the court held that the militants went in groups to different parts of the village, forced out the families after tying their hands, and killed most of the victims by cutting their throats, while some were shot. They also set fire to houses.

The doctors who examined the bodies told the trial court that they found incised wounds at the front of the neck, caused by a pasuli, and that some of the dead had firearm injuries. They carried out the post-mortems within a few hours, and the court found the timing consistent with the time of the attack.

The death toll is not given the same way everywhere. The Supreme Court spoke of 35 dead, and so did the Indian Express in the body of its 2016 article. The same article's summary line says 34. India Today in 1992 and Dalit Voice put it at 37. A writer in Round Table India gives 36. The sources do not explain these differences, so the figure of 35, the one the Supreme Court used, is the one that anchors this account.

Police submitted a charge sheet against 119 people, and a long list of prosecution witnesses was named. In the end, 13 people were tried by the Sessions Judge at Gaya, who was sitting as a designated court under TADA. The Supreme Court recorded that the prosecution examined 34 witnesses. The trial took about nine years, a length the later appeal to the Bihar chief minister described.

The verdict came on 8 June 2001. The court sentenced four men to death for terrorism offences, which the law then allowed: Nanhe Lal Mochi, Krishna Mochi, Bir Kuer Paswan and Dharmendra Singh. They had also been convicted of murder and given life terms. Four others, Bihari Manjhi, Ramautar Dusadh, Rajendra Paswan and Wakil Yadav, received life imprisonment. Ravindra Singh was given ten years under a separate provision of the anti-terror law, and did not appeal. Four accused were acquitted.

Round Table India describes the four as three Dalits and one Rajput, Dharmendra Singh. The People's Union for Democratic Rights (PUDR) says three of them came from landless Dalit families and had worked as harwahas, or farm labourers, before arrest.

TADA allowed no appeal to the High Court, so the case went straight to the Supreme Court as an appeal, together with the reference needed to confirm a death sentence. On 15 April 2002 Justice B. N. Agrawal wrote the judgment. He called it a case of "gruesome carnage" in which 35 members of a once powerful community were massacred, and he described the background as an outburst of caste war between "haves and have nots".

The defence argued that the prosecution had not proved the men's participation by credible evidence. It argued also that the informant, Sharma, had never been examined, so his first report could not be used as proof. And it argued that, where so many people were involved, the usual practice was to convict only on the consistent account of two or three witnesses. The court rejected the argument about the informant: even if the first report was not proved, it said, that would not be a ground for acquittal. On the witnesses, it went through the evidence one appellant at a time and recorded the number it found credible. For Krishna Mochi it counted four witnesses, for Dharmendra Singh one, for Nanhe Lal Mochi five and for Bir Kuer Paswan two.

On sentence, the defence argued the case was not one of the rarest of the rare. The court cited earlier rulings, including Bachan Singh and Machhi Singh, and then held that the conspiracy, the planning, the police uniforms, the tying of the victims and the killing of the helpless in great numbers placed the case in that category. The appeal was dismissed and the reference accepted: the death sentences were confirmed.

PUDR, in later statements, said the court was divided, with a two-member majority upholding the death penalty and a third judge dissenting, who would have acquitted Dharmendra Singh and given the other three life imprisonment. It also said the Supreme Court had noted weaknesses in the way TADA was applied.

Jail officials at Bhagalpur told the Indian Express that the four men's mercy petitions were sent to the President on 3 March 2003. A jail official, Vira Maharaj, said that once a petition is sent, the jail learns its status only when it is rejected. PUDR said the petitions were framed in 2003 but were not sent to the proper authorities for over ten years, and called that delay wilful negligence. The jail account and the PUDR account are not easy to reconcile, and neither is proved by the other source.

The Indian Express visited the families in 2016. Krishna Mochi, then 58, was in Bhagalpur jail, about 225 km from his village, and his youngest son, Ajay, whose mother was pregnant when Krishna was sentenced, said he had never seen his father. Ajay said he had been told his father was an excellent clarinet player, and the family said Krishna had belonged to a village wedding band. Bir Kuer Paswan was then 70. The families of Nanhe Lal and Bugal Mochi had moved away after their houses in Dhiwra village were set on fire in 1994, allegedly by upper-caste men. The paper reported that relatives did not know the status of the cases and relied on a lawyer who spoke sometimes of relief from Delhi and sometimes from Patna.

A group of academics and activists, including the economist Jean Dreze, wrote to the Chief Minister of Bihar asking for the four to be released. Their letter said the men had never been granted parole, that two of them were not allowed to attend their wives' last rites, and that by then two had served over 23 years and the others 18 and 17. They argued that the death penalty fell on the extremely poor and Dalits, citing the 2015 Law Commission report on the death penalty, and that TADA had lapsed in 1995 yet its harsh features, such as confessions made to police, the denial of bail and the denial of an appeal to a High Court, had been applied in this trial.

The critics' sharpest point was the contrast with cases in which Dalits were the victims. PUDR, citing its 2016 report Harvesting Death, said the Ranvir Sena, a caste army of upper-caste landlords, was responsible for 23 mass killings in which 256 poor and Dalit people died. In four of those cases, Bathani Tola, Laxmanpur-Bathe, Nagari Bazaar and Miyanpur, 125 accused were tried under ordinary law. According to PUDR, lower courts acquitted 56 and the Patna High Court later acquitted 68 for lack of evidence, and in the Nagari case only one person got life imprisonment. The Indian Express reported that in the Laxmanpur-Bathe case the Patna High Court acquitted all 26 upper-caste accused, whom a lower court had convicted, on grounds of inadequate evidence.

PUDR called Bara the only massacre case in which TADA was applied and upheld. It also argued that the case against the four rested on shoddy evidence: the first account was given by one eyewitness naming 35 people and others, and that witness was never produced in court. Round Table India made a similar argument, writing that TADA never gets applied when Dalits are massacred. These are the views of the critics. The Supreme Court had found the evidence of the witnesses it relied on to be credible and had rejected the objection about the informant.

From the first weeks there were rival explanations of who was behind the killings. India Today reported that the general suspicion was that Yadav leaders had engineered the massacre to teach the Bhumihars a lesson for opposing reservations and backing the Congress party. It quoted a Congress MLA, Hemant Shahi, who said it was wrong to blame the MCC alone because Yadav leaders had openly preached that Bhumihars should be taught a lesson. The magazine noted that the MCC did not own up to the killings and that some Congress leaders believed the MCC was led by Yadavs with links to Janata Dal leaders. It also reported that Chief Minister Yadav replied that police could not prevent such mayhem unless the root causes were removed. These were suspicions reported by a magazine, and the courts did not make findings on them.

A very different reading came from Dalit Voice, an outlet of Dalit politics, which published a piece on the killings. It described the dead as 37 Bhumihar Brahmins, rejected the labels Maoist and Naxalite for the attackers, and called the killings a retaliation against caste violence. That piece is advocacy and opinion, and is one of the reactions to the massacre. It stands opposite the Supreme Court's finding that the men who were tried belonged to the MCC.

A second trial followed. In 2009 the designated TADA judge at Gaya sentenced three more men, Vyas Kahar, Naresh Paswan and Bugal Mochi, to death, according to the Indian Express. Naresh was later acquitted, on grounds of lack of evidence and a shoddy investigation, in 2013. The sentences of Vyas and Bugal were reduced to life imprisonment, which PUDR says the Supreme Court did in 2013 and defined as imprisonment for the rest of their natural life.

The four men condemned in 2001 waited longer. By 31 January 2017 the President had commuted their death sentences, according to a statement from PUDR published that day; the saved sources give no earlier date. The group welcomed it but called it justice half done: the four, it said, would remain in jail with no clarity about the terms of commutation, and it called for the release of all six convicted in the case. It said the four had told its activists in 2015, on a visit to Bhagalpur jail, that they would rather die than spend the rest of their lives there.
content.h2: What is settled and what is not
content.p: The court record establishes a few points. A large group of armed people killed dozens of men in Bara on the night of 12 to 13 February 1992. The Supreme Court held that 35 died, that the attackers were members of the MCC and that the killings were planned. Four men were sentenced to death, had those sentences confirmed on appeal, and later had them commuted.

Other points are still contested. The sources disagree on the toll and on why the mercy petitions took so long to reach the President, and on whether a trial under a lapsed terror law could be fair. Only PUDR says the apex court was divided; the judgment saved here records only the majority opinion. The court's account attributes the attack to the MCC, and the political theories reported in 1992 appear only as press reports and politicians' claims.
